reviews.review:
I'm going to start this review with how impressed I am at this game's optimization. I have a crappy PC with a dual core processor, and this game is frequently hitting 60 fps with some infrequent stuttering here and there when the particle effects and environments get a little thick. Even at the lowest graphical settings, this game still looks good, so props to Relic on making this run like a dream on PC.

Now, to the review proper. A lot of 3rd person shooters focus far too much on stale cover-based shooting, ever since Gears of War did it relatively okay. Space Marine says to hell with cover and lets you tromp around and stomp the living ♥♥♥♥ out of xenos and heretics while using movement to keep yourself alive.

It uses a system where you have regenerating shields, but your actual health has to be recovered by getting into the thick of things and execute enemies when they're stunned. You need to make intelligent use of your dodges and know when to stun certain enemies and keep them out of combat while you work on the other guys in melee. While the combos themselves aren't particularly complex or challenging, they provide a surprising depth in your approach to close combat.

As for the shooting, Space Marine gets it right. If you're going to commit yourself to mid or long-range combat, you need to be constantly mindful of what pillars or walls you can use to peek around and use to run through, breaking up the enemy's fire. You can't just sit in once place forever, since the AI will know what you're trying to pull, and will make use of grenades to get you in their line of fire. They will also attempt to flank you and surround you all of the time.

This, combined with the melee combat system, makes for an actually challenging game that has you constantly scanning your surroundings and flushing out your enemies. There's hardly ever a dull moment, and each encounter tests you on what you've been learning throughout the game. While newbies are going to be frantically hunting for a spot to rest and be on edge in every battle, more experienced players can make it look hilariously easy.

Sound Design

The bolters are so damn punchy in this game. Everything is punchy. Even the steps taken by you and your fellow space marines sound massive and thud like you'd expect. Every aspect of this game sounds authentic, and never leaves you dissatisfied. This is also part of what keeps the shooting aspect of the game so fun, as the bolter makes thunderous noise and your enemies blow apart in juicy blood splatters.

When it comes to the narrative, it is standard 40k fare, but the characters themselves are, for me, the most memorable thing in the story. Mark Strong does a great job voicing Captain Titus, and the captain himself is a pretty badass dude. The Ultramarines are often mocked as ponces and an obnoxious, uptight chapter. While this does hold true in many cases, Titus shows the best attributes of the chapter, and embodies the ideals of his primarch. Hell, I'd say the guy is the spitting image of Guilliman.

Sidonus is a cool guy, Leandros is a whipped little ♥♥♥♥♥, the Blood Ravens make an appearance along with the Black Templars, the IG is as manly as ever, and the the chaos lord is actually kind of cool; while he doesn't match up to the likes of Eliphas, he's still leagues better than other chaos lords we've seen in the past. The ork warboss, Grimskull, is probably one of my favorite orks ever, right behind Gorgutz 'Ead 'Unter.

Overall, I'd say that this is a game that certainly does 40k justice, and is a great starting point for anyone who wants to get more into the lore side of the setting. As a game, it's pretty damn good, and keeps me coming back constantly with its campaign and multiplayer. I would love to see Relic revisit Space Marine sometime in the near future, and finish it off proper, since the cliffhanger at the end is downright criminal. So, yes, I do recommend Space Marine.

Here's the thing.

I quite like this game. I like the setting, I like the shooty shoots and the hit hits, I like how the story is nonexistent, how the plot is as cliche 40k as they come, how the Thunder Hammer absolutely destroys once you get it, and how your big meaty boots shake the ground when you run. I like a lot about this game. There are two fundamental design flaws that ruin the experience, though, and I cannot recommend this game to anyone unless you are willing to put up with incredible frustration. They are:

--In melee: enemies will stun you, but you do not stunlock enemies (during normal attacks)
--Your dodge roll and execution animations do not have any invincibility frames.

These pretty much ruin the actual gameplay experience. Add to that your surprisingly low health and shield bar and the propensity for the game to load encounters with RocketBoyz past the 6th chapter or so, and pretty soon the game becomes a frustrating slog that never quite feels fair. 

Fighting bigger enemies is frustrating because you can't stunlock them and do damage at the same time, but they can stun you through your attack animation. Eventually you'll learn the only way to beat them is by stunning them over and over for a minute or so (as stuns do little damage) and waiting for the little "execution" prompt to appear; during this time you may be getting wrecked my melee Orks or RocketBoyz. Eventually you may decide to  just hang back and bullet-sponge them into oblivion--considering your weapons are inherently innacurate and shooting isn't the focus, this is a real drag.

If the Dodge Roll actually worked, this might not be a problem. It doesn't. Unlike plenty of other slash-em-ups (God of War, DMC, etc., Dark Souls), there are no i-frames (that I can tell) in a roll. As a result, there's no point in dodging: you'll still be hit during the dodge, and more often that not it will just propel into further danger. Enemies have long-range melee attacks, and most arenas are so small you'll end up getting caught on the claustrophobic level design. Add to that the fact you're probably being peppered by impossibly accurate ranged Orks and a limited health bar and you may just give up entirely.

Finally, the execution system. The only way to regain health in this game is by "executing" enemies with a stylish animation. This is awesome in theory and brutal and fun in practice. During the actual animation, though, you'll still take damage; and, considering you're effectively standing still during this time, you'll be taking a LOT of damage. It defeats the purpose of a melee system entirely: it's better to just stay back and let Orks soak up an astonishing amount of bullets rather than risk getting killed trying to regain health after you've had your chainsword fun. And when checkpoints start getting wonky and put you behind not one but two enemy encounters every time your die, you'll really start to resent the unfair deaths.

So there it is. There are other problems with the game (they could have removed RocketBoyz entirely and the game would have been better for it), but I still enjoyed myself while the fun lasted. At least play until you get the Thunder Hammer, because that's a blast. And maybe try playing on Easy your first time (I wasn't able to tell the difference between Easy and Normal, but at least Easy may get rid of more frustrating deaths). Oh, and that first Ork Boss? Probably the worst boss design I've encountered in a long time. It doesn't really telegraph what you're supposed to you, how you're supposed to do it, floods the arena with enemies, and gives the boss an almost one-hit kill that's hard to dodge. Yup.

But then again Jim Sterling thought it wasn't bad, so maybe give it a shot. Jim is pretty good at gauging when games are too frustrating to play. Maybe I just sucked at this one. PS: Nvidia cards are known to have problems. I have a 750 Ti and it had graphical glitches from time to time that required a force restart. YMMV.

UPDATE: Playing the game through on Easy is way better, and that boss is a cakewalk if you happen to bring along a Melta-Gun. I didn't my first time, and the checkpoint is after you have the opportunity to pick one up so there's no way to go back and change your mind. In general, any time you're presented with weapons in the game you'll never know which ones to pick, and certain encounters are CLEARLY designed for specific weapons. This, I think, contributed to the game being very easy fro some people and very hard for others. The review stands.

TL;DR:

Space Marine is a flawed game; it has a lot of bits and pieces that don't quite line up. Nonetheless, I had a lot of fun playing through the short campaign (about 8 hours), and I spent plenty of time on the almost-dead multiplayer modes. At its core, the gameplay is solid, and satisfying enough to make up for many of its other shortcomings. Space Marine is easier to recommend to fans of the Warhammer 40,000 universe who will be able to pull more out of the bland story and multiplayer customizations, but even non-fans can enjoy the short run through the campaign if they just want a simple, and fun action game.

Read the full review here: http://dagondogs.com/2016/02/24/space-marine-late-bird-review/

This game is a lot of fun.  If you are a 40K fan, then it should already be part of your collection.  If you enjoy general awesomeness, blood, gore, or are desirous of a greater quantity of chest hair, you should consider getting this game.  The single player is a romp with easy replayablitiy.  The multiplayer is fairly dynamic, with good variety if you can find an ongoing game (which can sometimes be difficult).  The only real drag is the Ultramarines, but that's what mods are for, and the multiplayer customiser is simply superb.  10/10 Would Let the Galaxy Burn/The Emperor Protect again.
